name: Unity
tagline: Cross-platform game engine and editor for 2D, 3D, mobile, console and XR titles.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Unity Personal is free under a revenue threshold, Pro is a paid annual per-seat license.

verdictSummary: Unity is not an app, it is twenty years of renderer, physics, asset pipeline, and platform export work with a scripting runtime bolted on top. An agent can absolutely give you a scene graph, a transform gizmo, and a play button in an afternoon, and it will feel great for about a day. Then you want a lightmapper, an animation state machine, a mobile build that does not stutter, a console SDK you legally cannot touch, and 40,000 Asset Store packages you were quietly planning to use. Also worth noting Unity Personal is free for most individuals, so the thing you would be replacing costs nothing until you are making real money. Build a toy engine to learn, not to migrate.
coreLoopDIY: A browser-based 3D scene editor: add primitives and glTF models, move them with gizmos, attach small script components, save the scene as JSON, and hit play to run physics and input.
requirements: Three.js plus a physics library like Rapier
whatYouLose: Platform export: consoles, mobile stores, XR headsets, all with signed toolchains
The Asset Store, which is most of how real projects actually ship
Baked lighting, occlusion culling, animation state machines, particle systems, terrain
A profiler that tells you why the frame took 40ms
Every tutorial, forum answer and hireable developer who already knows the editor
moatNotes: The engine itself is only half of it. The other half is that every artist, plugin author and console vendor already targets it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly they do not, at first: Personal is free until revenue clears the threshold, which is exactly the point. By the time you are paying for Pro, you have a team, a shipping deadline, a console port, and thirty paid packages wired into your project. Nobody switches engines at that stage for philosophical reasons, and nobody ships a commercial title on a hand-rolled renderer unless the renderer is the product. The license fee is cheaper than one month of an engine programmer.
notes: A weekend scene editor teaches you a lot and ships nothing. The moat is the platform toolchains plus an asset marketplace and a labor pool that both assume Unity by default.
prompt:
Build a browser-based 3D scene editor and runtime. This is a learning toy, not a Unity replacement, and the README should say so.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + TypeScript, no framework, plain DOM for the UI
- Three.js for rendering, WebGPU renderer with a WebGL fallback
- @dimforge/rapier3d-compat for physics
- No backend, no accounts, no telemetry. Scenes persist to IndexedDB and export as JSON files.

Editor requirements:
- Layout: left hierarchy panel, center viewport, right inspector panel, bottom log console
- Orbit camera, grid, infinite ground plane toggle
- Add primitives: box, sphere, capsule, plane, directional light, point light
- Import .glb via drag and drop, store the file bytes in IndexedDB
- Selection with click and outline highlight, TransformControls gizmo with translate/rotate/scale modes on keys W/E/R
- Inspector edits name, transform, material color, cast/receive shadow, and physics body type: none, static, dynamic
- Undo/redo stack for add, delete, and transform, at least 50 steps
- Save/Load/New scene, plus Export JSON and Import JSON

Runtime requirements:
- Play/Stop toggle. Play snapshots the scene, runs a fixed 60Hz Rapier step, Stop restores the snapshot exactly
- A minimal component system: each object can have a list of scripts chosen from a built-in registry, not eval'd user code. Ship four: Spin, FollowMouse, WASDCharacter, KillOnFall
- Scripts get onStart and onUpdate(dt) with access to the object and an input state object

Explicitly out of scope, note this in the README: baked lighting, animation blending, terrain tools, prefabs, asset store, any native or mobile export.

Deliver: npm install && npm run dev works from a clean clone, a demo scene that loads on first run showing a dynamic ball rolling into stacked boxes, and a README with the scene JSON schema documented.
